topic: burning lime in a small field kiln: stone size, draught, burn temperature and slaking to putty

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-4)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: kiln pyrometer z sonda; referent nieosadzony 'signal relay' z innej dziedziny technicznej

base: I have rebuilt a small field kiln and want to burn my own lime.
An older kiln sits half collapsed in the next field and burned well once.
A kiln pyrometer with a long probe now reads the burn every ten minutes.
My first burn left a lot of raw stone in the middle of the charge.
Is my stone too large, or did the draught never reach the centre?
Raw stone in the middle nearly always means the draught failed to get through.
Break the stone to an even size, roughly a fist across at most.
Mixed sizes pack together and close the gaps that carry heat upward.
Build the charge in layers with the fuel spread evenly through each one.
Breaking the stone evenly has changed everything and the last burn ran hot.
The charge glowed right through and very little raw stone came out.
The kiln pyrometer showed eleven hundred degrees for most of the second night.
Is that hotter than I need, or about right for burning good lime?
Eleven hundred is a shade hot, since nine hundred will drive the stone.
Too much heat starts to sinter the surface and the lime slakes badly afterwards.
Hold the burn nearer a thousand and simply carry it on for longer.
Time at heat matters far more than the highest number you ever reach.
Holding a thousand degrees for two days gave a much softer and chalkier lump.
The lump fizzes hard in water and throws off a great deal of heat.
The older kiln in the next field had a much narrower throat than mine.
Should I narrow my own throat, or leave the kiln exactly as it stands?
Leave the throat alone, because a narrow one suits coal rather than wood.
Wood needs a wider opening to carry the flame up through the charge.
Turn now to the slaking, which decides more about your lime than the burn.
Add the lump to water, never water to the lump, and stand well back.
Slaking into a butt of water gave a thick and creamy putty.
Some lumps sank to the bottom and sat there without breaking down at all.
The putty smells sharp and warms the side of the butt for hours.
Are those sunken lumps wasted, or will they slake given enough time?
Sunken lumps are usually overburned and they will never slake properly at all.
Screen the putty through a coarse sieve before you store it in the butt.
A lump left in the putty will blow a hole in your plaster later.
Keep the putty under two inches of water and let it mature quietly.
I screened the whole butt and the putty is smooth right through now.
It has stood three months under water and feels stiffer than at first.
A skin has formed on the surface wherever the water level dropped.
Is that skin a loss, or can I stir it back into the putty?
Skim the skin off and throw it away, because it has already carbonated.
Stirred back in, it leaves hard specks that show up badly in fine work.
Top the water up every month and the skin will hardly form again.
Putty kept a full year under water works far sweeter under the trowel.
